newsitem.title: FRANCE: Analysts pan Thomson-CSF halt, stock hit.
newsitem.headline: Analysts pan Thomson-CSF halt, stock hit.

text.p: Defence and stock analysts on Tuesday criticised France's decision to axe the privatisation of Thomson-CSF, saying it appeared to have put short-term defence of sovereignty and jobs above European alliances.

Shares in Europe's leading defence electronics manufacturer fell by almost six percent as investors reacted badly to Friday's announcement following a long holiday weekend. At 1145 GMT Thomson-CSF was down 10.1 francs at 159.5.
Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, elected last month, halted the sale of the state's 58 percent stake planned by his predecessors saying it was not in the country's interests.
But analysts said the move showed Jospin misunderstood the dynamics of the fast-moving global defence industry.
"Industrially and financially we don't really understand the logic of this," said Emmanuel Dubois-Pelerin, analyst with Standard & Poor's in Paris.

"They are favouring national and short-term interests rather than industrial and long-term interests. They think they can combine these two and I'm not sure they perceive the contradictions," he said.
Analysts outside France were even harsher.

"You can't overstate the problems this is going to cause. This is a demonstration that the French are not interested in restructuring the European defence sector on commercial grounds," said Paul Beaver of Jane's Defence Weekly.
The analysts said a future French defence giant could face problems forging alliances with private companies in the rest of Europe if the government were seen to control decision-making.

"The biggest obstacle the government has put in the way of Thomson-CSF becoming a major and efficient player in the world industry is maintaining their presence in the company's capital," Dubois-Pelerin said.
The government has not said what it means by its intention to keep a "decisive" stake in Thomson-CSF, but has indicated it will keep a significant chunk of the equity in state hands.

Dubois-Pelerin said building a French defence combine from a combination of Thomson-CSF, Alcatel, warplane maker Dassault Aviation and state-owned planemaker Aerospatiale -- one possibility for an internal restructuring -- would result in an "extremely awkward" share structure.
Analysts said the government's decision did not totally dash industry hopes of wider European restructuring to tackle transatlantic competition after a series of U.S. mega-mergers.
"It doesn't eliminate the likelihood that something big will get done in the European industry but it addes a complicating factor," Dubois-Pelerin said.
